description: Industry-specific Financial Health Score (0-100). Five pillars with declared point budgets; each metric is scored by its percentile among industry peers (sector, or the industry framework for financial companies), capped by absolute guardrails so that a weak company cannot score well just because its peers are weak. Budgets and metric weights are a declared design (not fitted to any outcome); see docs/HEALTH_SCORE_FRAMEWORK.md for the rationale, validation and sensitivity analysis. Missing data never receives points: it lowers the confidence and, below the minimums, withholds the score.

operating_income_cagr.name: Operating income growth (CAGR, up to 3 years)

net_income_cagr.name: Net income growth (CAGR, up to 3 years)

guardrails_note: Absolute floors that override peer-relative points (conventional credit-analysis thresholds; e.g. Damodaran's synthetic-rating table assigns sub-investment-grade ratings below ~1.5-2x interest coverage, and loan covenants commonly cap net debt/EBITDA at 3-4x). A guardrail can only LOWER points, never raise them.

it_services.label: Information technology
it_services.efficiency_note: IT and software companies carry little or no inventory; collection of receivables (days sales outstanding) is their working-capital driver, so receivables turnover replaces inventory turnover.

energy.label: Energy (oil, gas, coal)
energy.growth_note: Energy revenue follows commodity prices: growth is scored against energy peers in the same years, never against technology companies.

utilities.label: Utilities (regulated, capital-intensive)
utilities.note: Utilities run with high, stable leverage and current ratios below 1 (regulated cash flows), so leverage is judged against utility peers against utility peers and no current-ratio floor; free cash flow is often negative during capital programmes.

real_estate.label: Real estate
real_estate.note: Property portfolios and project inventories turn over slowly by nature, so efficiency is asset turnover against real-estate peers only; high leverage is normal for REITs and developers and is judged against real-estate peers.

banking.label: Banking

LIQUIDITY.not_assessed: Bank liquidity needs deposits, liquid assets and regulatory ratios (LCR/NSFR), which the data provider does not report. Working-capital ratios do not apply to banks.

EFFICIENCY.not_assessed: Bank efficiency is measured by the cost-to-income ratio and asset quality (gross/net NPA, provision coverage), which the data provider does not report consistently.

banking.note: Equity / total assets is a simple leverage-based capital buffer, not the regulatory capital adequacy ratio (CET1/CRAR, which risk-weights assets). Profitability uses ROA (the standard bank return measure) rather than ROE, which mostly reflects leverage.

guardrails.reason: equity below 4% of assets (thin capital buffer)

insurance.label: Insurance

LIQUIDITY.not_assessed: Insurer liquidity depends on the duration match of investments and policy liabilities, which the data provider does not report.

EFFICIENCY.not_assessed: Insurer efficiency is measured by the combined and expense ratios, which need premium and claims data the provider does not report.

insurance.note: Return on equity is the conventional insurer profitability measure; equity / assets approximates the solvency buffer, not the regulatory solvency ratio.

financial_services.label: Other financial services (NBFCs, capital markets, asset managers)

LIQUIDITY.not_assessed: Lender and broker liquidity needs asset-liability maturity data the provider does not report.

EFFICIENCY.not_assessed: Efficiency of lenders and asset managers (cost-to-income, credit costs, assets under management) is not reported by the provider.

guardrails.reason: equity below 8% of assets for a non-bank lender

redundancy_rule: Metrics sharing a pillar must have |Spearman rho| < 0.7 over the universe (checked by the calibration). Net debt / EBITDA was replaced by the debt ratio because its correlation with interest coverage was -0.72 (double counting); the debt ratio's is -0.51.
